culturalStory.heading: About the Raven
body: The raven (kahkakiw) holds significant cultural importance in many Indigenous traditions, including Plains Cree (nēhiyawēwin). Known for its intelligence, adaptability, problem-solving ability, and distinctive black plumage and rasping call, the raven appears in numerous oral stories and teachings.

In Cree storytelling the raven is often a trickster and messenger figure — a bird that watches, remembers, and carries news between worlds. This trail sign honours that presence with a stylized black raven silhouette and the syllabics ᑲᐦᑲᑭᐤ set across its body in red, so that the Cree name is literally carried on the raven itself.

culturalStory.heading: Spine of the Trail
body: In mountain-bike vernacular, a trail earns the name Back Breaker by feel — by the rooty, rattling sections that hammer your spine through the bars, by the line that punishes a lazy posture and rewards a loose grip. The trail of that name drops through MacKinnon Ravine on Edmonton's west side as the rooty companion to Root Canal: short, sharp, and unforgiving enough that the name has stuck for years among the local riders who built and maintain it.

The plaque leans into the joke literally. A single white vertebra dangles like a charm against the black field, ringed with red the way a sore spine glows after a hard run. The accompanying parts in this sign's set — a five-vertebra column and a length of chain — push the pun further: a backbone built like a bike chain, each link a vertebra, the rider's spine and the bike's drivetrain merged into one rattling assembly. Red on black is the working-shop palette of grease, rust, and warning tape; the white SRO and English text keep the language clearly legible against it.

The Cree reading kaskâwikanênêw carries that same idea in its own register — a verb built from kaskâ‑ ‘to snap, break across’ and the body-part medial ‑wikan‑ ‘back, spine’: literally, ‘s/he breaks his/her back (by hand).’ The syllabics above the SRO are picked out in the same red as the vertebra's accents, so the language and the image read as a single gesture. The sign sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), and is part of an Edmonton-area effort to put Plains Cree names back on the everyday landscape of trails that riders here have known by their English nicknames for a long time.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'kaskâwikanênêw' (circumflex on the third 'a') and syllabics 'ᑲᐢᑳᐏᑲᓀᓀᐤ' (long-â dot on the third glyph ᑳ). The current catalogue.json has 'kaskawikanênêw' / 'ᑲᐢᑲᐏᑲᓀᓀᐤ' — both missing the long-â diacritic in matched positions. The plaque is internally consistent and matches the itwêwina (Wolvengrey/CW) headword 'kaskâwikanênêw' = 's/he breaks s.o.’s back by hand'. Coordinator should update catalogue.json creeName + creeSyllabics to match the plaque when merging.

culturalStory.heading: About mistâpiskihkomân — the Big Iron Knife
body: On the wall the mistâpiskihkomân plaque is one of the most graphic in the set: a single black machete blade laid across the white plaque, its metal painted matte and its handle riveted, with the syllabics ᒥᐢᑖᐱᐢᑭᐦᑯᒫᐣ carved in red right down the spine of the blade. The English word ‘MACHETE’ underneath the knife is large and unambiguous — there is no joke here, just a sharp tool named in two languages.

The Cree word is a stack of three productive parts. mist‑ means ‘big, great’ (the same initial in mistik ‘big tree’, mistatim ‘horse / great-dog’, and mistahi ‘a lot’). ‑âpisk‑ is the body-part-style medial for ‘of metal, of iron, of stone’ (the same medial in many tool words). And ‑(i)hkomân is the knife-final, the same root that surfaces independently as môhkomân ‘knife.’ Read together the word is literally ‘the great iron knife’ — exactly what a machete is, in three Cree morphemes.

The trail itself drops through Keillor in NW Edmonton on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory): rough, loose, and quick, with steep drops and tight corners — Trailforks lists it as black diamond. The plaque’s naming choice mirrors the trail’s feel: where a small knife (môhkomân) is for fine work, the big iron knife is for clearing line through the brush. The red syllabics on the black blade let the language stay legible at distance, the way a warning sign should.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE (syllabics): The plaque is carved with SRO 'mistâpiskihkomân' (matches catalogue) but with syllabics 'ᒥᐢᑖᐱᐢᑭᐦᑯᒫᐣ' — note the long-â glyph ᑖ on the second position. The current catalogue.json creeSyllabics is 'ᒥᐢᑕᐱᐢᑭᐦᑯᒫᐣ' (with short-a ᑕ instead of ᑖ). Trailforks's AKA listing for trail #30260 also writes ᒥᐢᑖᐱᐢᑭᐦᑯᒫᐣ. Coordinator should update catalogue creeSyllabics to ᒥᐢᑖᐱᐢᑭᐦᑯᒫᐣ.

Morpheme bracketing of mist‑âpisk‑ihkomân is the standard teaching analysis (size-initial + metal-medial + knife-final). An alternative analysis treats the word as mist‑ + âpiskihkomân (a single nominalized stem 'iron-knife') for fluency-level speakers; the three-morpheme split is preferred here for teaching clarity and to surface the ‑âpisk‑ metal medial which appears in many other tool words.
The ‑(i)hkomân final is the bound form of free môhkomân 'knife'. The vowel quality difference (ô- vs. -i-) is a regular Cree phonological alternation in compound stems.

culturalStory.heading: About nikocwâsaskanôs — the Little Six-Shot
body: On the wall the nikocwâsaskanôs plaque sits directly under the mistâpiskihkomân (Machete) plaque, sharing the same white-and-black palette: a long single-action revolver in black silhouette with a bone-handle grip, the syllabics ᓂᑯᒑᐧᓴᐢᑲᓅᐢ carved in red across the chamber, and ‘SIX SHOOTER’ in big letters underneath.

The Cree word reads three pieces deep. nikocwâs‑ is the numeral ‘six’ (the standard nikotwâsik, with the local Plains Cree palatalisation tw → cw that you hear across Edmonton). ‑askan‑ is the body-part medial ‘bone, hard projecting thing,’ the same medial in oskan ‘bone’; here it names the cylinder-and-barrel as the gun’s hard six-piece. The diminutive ‑ôs at the end means ‘small, little.’ Read together: ‘the little six-shot.’

The trail of the same name flows along the south side of the river toward Emily Murphy Park in NW Edmonton. Trailforks rates it blue with a 1.1 km roll-and-pump style, named — like its neighbours Rich Kid, Plan B, and Machete — in the cowboy/outlaw register that the local builders favour for this stretch. The land is ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), and Trailforks itself lists the AKA ᓂᑯᒑᐧᓴᐢᑲᓅᐢ nikocwâsaskanôs for this trail — the same form carved on the plaque.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE (syllabics): The plaque carving and Trailforks both write the syllabics as 'ᓂᑯᒑᐧᓴᐢᑲᓅᐢ' (with ᒑᐧ for cwâ and ᓅ for nô). The current catalogue creeSyllabics 'ᓂᑯᐚᓴᐢᑲᓄᐢ' is missing the c-glyph and the long-ô on the diminutive. Coordinator should update catalogue creeSyllabics to ᓂᑯᒑᐧᓴᐢᑲᓅᐢ. The catalogue creeName 'nikocwâsaskanôs' is already correct.

Morpheme bracketing nikocwâs‑askan‑ôs is the structural reading: numeral six + bone-medial + diminutive. An alternative reading parses the word as nikocwâs‑askanôs where ‑askanôs is a frozen ‘small bone-thing’ noun; both readings yield the same surface form, but the three-morpheme split is preferred here because the ‑askan‑ medial is independently productive in Cree word-formation (as in oskan).
The cw cluster in nikocwâsaskanôs reflects the local Plains Cree palatalisation of tw → cw (so nikotwâsik ‘six’ → nikocwâsik). Both forms are widely heard across nehiyaw-askiy.
The diminutive ‑ôs is a regular Plains Cree diminutive ending; for animate nouns ‑sis is more common. Here the gun is grammatically inanimate (NI), so ‑ôs is the expected ending.

Trailforks pick: 'Six Shooter' (trail id 18858), Central Edmonton (South) / NW Edmonton — blue singletrack. Trailhead 53.52434, -113.54104. High confidence (Trailforks lists AKA ᓂᑯᒑᐧᓴᐢᑲᓅᐢ nikocwâsaskanôs explicitly).

culturalStory.heading: About nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk — the Haze We Ride Through
body: Purple Haze is a Hendrix song before it is a trail, and the trail name is itself a borrow — when the local builders carved the Cree, they did not try to translate the colour ‘purple’ literally (which Plains Cree does not have a single root for) but instead rendered the FEELING of the song and the trail: the dim, hazy way of moving through. The plaque on the wall is unusually pictorial for the set: a two-tone purple mountain silhouette under a pink-fading-to-violet sky, the syllabics ᓂᐹᒫᔮᑖᐣ ᐯᑭᓭᔮᕽ in clean white above the mountain, ‘PURPLE HAZE’ in white block letters across the violet base.

The Cree breaks into two parts. nîpâmâyâtân is a VII (it-verb): nîpâ‑ ‘in the dark, at night, dimly’ + ‑mâyâtan ‘it is bad / ugly / unclear,’ together meaning roughly ‘it is hazy / dim / hard to see’ (the sense Hendrix gets at with ‘purple haze all in my eyes’). pekiseyâhk is an AI conjunct in the first-person-plural inclusive: ‘when we (all of us) pass through it.’ Read together: ‘when it is hazy and we (all) pass through it’ — the rider’s phrase, not a colour name.

The trail itself is in the Hawrelak/Central Edmonton (North) network, neighbour to Wonder Woman, Lovers Lane, and Victoria’s Secret in the river-valley clusters under ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). On the wall there are two Purple Haze plaques — a small portrait-format one in row 1 (the one wired here) and a fuller one further right — both reading the same Cree.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'nîpâmâyâtân pekiseyâhk' (with circumflex on the first î; final ‑hk on pekiseyâhk). The current catalogue creeName 'nipâmâyâtan pekisehyânik' is materially different — it is missing the î circumflex on the first vowel, missing the n-final on ‑mâyâtân, has a spurious ‑hy‑ in pekise(h)yâhk, and ends in ‑ânik instead of ‑yâhk. culturalStory.heading: About nicimos mêskanâs — My Sweetheart’s Little Path
body: Lovers Lane is the rare trail name where the English and the Cree mean almost exactly the same thing. The plaque is a red-on-white heart filled with three interlocking gear-discs, each carrying a piece of the syllabics ᓂᒋᒧᐢ ᒣᐢᑲᓈᐢ in white — when you read the gears in heart-shape order they spell the phrase. ‘nicimos mêskanâs’ runs across the top in plain SRO; ‘Lovers Lane’ runs across the bottom. Two of these heart plaques are mounted on the wall.

The Cree breaks into two short pieces. nicimos is the 1sg possessed form of ‑cimos ‘sweetheart, dear, lover’ — the dependent stem that always appears with a possessor prefix (nicimos ‘my sweetheart’, kicimos ‘your sweetheart’, ocimosa ‘his/her sweetheart (obviative)’). mêskanâs is the diminutive of mêskanaw ‘road, trail, path’: literally ‘little path.’ Together: ‘my sweetheart’s little path’ — the affectionate scale of a singletrack through the river-valley bush.

The trail itself is in the Central Edmonton (North) network, on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), near Government House just up the bank from the river. Trailforks describes it well: ‘single track that winds through tight overhanging bush creating a cool tunnel effect — rolls and flows well in both directions.’ It is a blue trail (also locally called ‘Groat Road Roller Coaster’ or ‘Monkey Trail’ in MTB vernacular) — the kind of soft, looping line that the Cree name dignifies as a path you’d take a sweetheart down.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'nicimos mêskanâs' (singular nicimos, NOT plural nicimosak; circumflex ê on mêskanâs, NOT acute é). The current catalogue creeName 'nicimosak méskanâs' has both errors — it pluralises the sweetheart and uses a French acute é instead of the Cree circumflex ê. Coordinator should update catalogue creeName to 'nicimos mêskanâs'.

PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE (syllabics): Catalogue creeSyllabics 'ᓂᒋᒧᓴᐠ ᒣᐢᑲᓈᐢ' encodes the broken plural form (note ‑ᓴᐠ ‘‑sak’ at the end of nicimos). The plaque-correct syllabics is 'ᓂᒋᒧᐢ ᒣᐢᑲᓈᐢ'. Coordinator should update creeSyllabics accordingly.

There is a possible carving variant nîcimos (with circumflex on the first î; itwêwina headword form). The carved plaque appears to use plain 'nicimos' (no î diacritic) — this is the form chosen here. Some Plains Cree dictionaries write nîcimos with long î; both are widely attested and the plaque’s short-i spelling is acceptable.

Morpheme bracketing ni‑ + cimos | mêskan‑ + ‑âs is the structural reading. cimos is a dependent NA stem that never surfaces without a possessive prefix (so ni‑cimos ‘my sweetheart,’ ki‑cimos ‘your sweetheart,’ etc.). mêskanâs is the regular NI diminutive of mêskanaw with the ‑âs ending and final-vowel reduction (mêskanaw → mêskan‑ + ‑âs).

High confidence (the trail page is a direct match for the carved Cree name, and the wall is clearly the Edmonton Plains Cree mountain-bike-naming project).

culturalStory.heading: About mamahtâw iskwew — the Wondrous Woman
body: The mamahtâw iskwew plaque turns the comic-book Wonder Woman into a nehiyaw (Plains Cree) figure. The black silhouette is unmistakable — the star tiara, the wave of hair, the lariat looped around both arms — but the syllabics across the torso, ᒪᒪᐦᑖᐤ ᐃᐢᑲᐧᐤ, render the name in a register the Amazonian original never had: mamahtâw is the same word the language uses for spirit-power, for healers, for people who do remarkable things. ‘Wondrous woman’ is the literal gloss; ‘miracle woman’ is closer to the cultural feel.

The phrase is a pre-noun + noun construction. mamahtâw is a VII (it-is-wondrous) used adjectivally before the noun: it does not inflect. iskwew is the everyday NA noun for ‘woman.’ The same root surfaces in the AI verb mamahtâwisiw ‘s/he has spirit-power, s/he does wondrous things,’ and in the abstract noun mamahtâwisiwin ‘miraculousness, spirit-power.’ The naming choice is deliberate: it lifts a pop-culture superhero into a category — the wondrous one, the one with spirit-power — that already exists in nehiyawêwin and that names actual people in Cree communities.

The trail itself is a 327 m stretch in the Hawrelak network on the south side of the river, in the same cluster as Lovers Lane, Victoria’s Secret, Purple Haze, and Back Breaker — short, blue-difficulty, tucked behind Government House and the Korean Pavilion. Trailforks itself lists the AKA mamahtâw iskwew for the trail. The land is ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). The plaque’s red syllabics on a black silhouette pop against the bare white background — language and image carrying the same idea in two scripts.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with SRO 'mamahtâw iskwew' (with circumflex on the â). The current catalogue creeName 'mamahtaw iskwew' is missing the â circumflex. Trailforks's AKA listing for trail #31377 also writes 'mamahtâw iskwew' (with â). Coordinator should update catalogue creeName to 'mamahtâw iskwew'.

PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE (syllabics): The carved syllabics shows the long-â glyph ᑖ (with dot above) in the fourth position of mamahtâw — i.e. 'ᒪᒪᐦᑖᐤ.' The current catalogue creeSyllabics 'ᒪᒪᐦᑕᐤ ᐃᐢᑲᐧᐤ' has plain ᑕ (short a) in that position. Coordinator should update creeSyllabics to ᒪᒪᐦᑖᐤ ᐃᐢᑲᐧᐤ.

Note the legacy folder name 'mamahtaw_askwew' contains a typo ('askwew' for 'iskwew'). The folder is not renamed (per coordinator instructions); the catalogue 'folder' field correctly points to the existing path. The PAGE displays the corrected 'iskwew' / ᐃᐢᑲᐧᐤ in all carved-text positions.

iskwew syllabics: the carved plaque uses the decomposed form 'ᐃᐢᑲᐧᐤ' (i + s + ka + w-medial + w-final). The unified-syllabic form 'ᐃᐢᑵᐤ' (i + s + kwê + w) is also valid and is what itwêwina uses. The page uses the carved decomposed form for fidelity to the plaque, but the related-forms section uses the unified form for the plural ᐃᐢᑵᐘᐠ where it reads more naturally.

Morpheme analysis treats mamahtâw as an indeclinable pre-noun (the VII bare stem used adjectivally) plus the NA noun iskwew. An alternative analysis writes it as a single compound 'mamahtâwiskwew' meaning ‘wondrous-woman’ (single word). Both readings are linguistically defensible; the two-word reading is preferred here because the plaque visually separates the words and Trailforks’s AKA also separates them.

Trailforks pick: 'Wonder Woman' (trail id 31377), Hawrelak / NW Edmonton — 327m blue singletrack with a black-diamond climb, behind Government House. Trailhead 53.54092, -113.54308. High confidence (Trailforks lists AKA ‘mamahtâw iskwew’).

culturalStory.heading: About the Ray Gun
body: The carved plaque reads sâpwâpahcikan pâskisikan — literally 'a through-shooting firearm', a tidy Cree neologism for the English mountain-bike trail nickname Ray Gun. The retro silver-on-white silhouette borrows from 1950s pulp sci-fi: thick grip, bell-mouth barrel, a red sound-wave radiating out into a single sharp dot at the end of the beam.

Cree readers will recognise pâskisikan as the everyday word for 'gun' — from pâskisikê‑ 'to discharge a firearm' plus the same instrumental ‑kan ending that builds masinahikan 'book' from 'writing'. The first word, sâpwâpahcikan, picks up the productive verb initial sâpw‑ 'through, all the way through' — the same initial behind sâpwâstê 'a beam of light shines through' — and pairs it with an instrument ending. Together the two words name the trail as 'a firearm that shoots beams through everything.'

sâpwâpahcikan pâskisikan sits in the third row of the wall, just left of capanaskos / Bobsled, and is part of the same Kinsmen / Emily Murphy Park run that includes nikocwâsaskanôs / Six Shooter and sôniyâwâhkêsis / Silverfox. The signs are part of an Edmonton-area effort to put Plains Cree (nēhiyawēwin) names back on the everyday landscape of trails that riders here have known by their English nicknames for a long time. Plaque text colours: black SRO on white, red Cree syllabics, red ray-gun silhouette with the single beam-dot at the tip.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The plaque is carved with circumflex on the second word — pâskisikan (â over the first 'a'). The current catalogue has paskisikan (no diacritic). Coordinator should update catalogue.json creeName 'sâpwâpahcikan paskisikan' → 'sâpwâpahcikan pâskisikan', and creeSyllabics 'ᓵᐚᐸᐦᒋᑲᐣ ᐸᐢᑭᓯᑲᐣ' → 'ᓵᐚᐸᐦᒋᑲᐣ ᐹᐢᑭᓯᑲᐣ' (ᐸ → ᐹ in the second word).

sâpwâpahcikan appears to be an author-coined Cree neologism rather than a stock dictionary entry. The morpheme split sâpw‑ ‘through’ + ‑âp‑ ‘see/beam’ + ‑ahcikan ‘instrumental nominalizer’ is the most defensible reading, but a stricter parse may collapse ‑âp‑ahcikan as a single ‑(âp)ahcike‑ derivation. Either reading is linguistically defensible — flagged for elder/curator review.

culturalStory.heading: Springs Underfoot
body: The plaque does not name a single Cree word for 'bed-spring' — there isn't one in everyday speech. Instead the carving spells out a small descriptive sentence: nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak, literally 'a bed (a sleeping-place), the thing(s) that bounce.' It is the kind of phrase a Cree speaker might construct on the fly to describe a piece of unfamiliar furniture, and it preserves that exploratory, fitted-to-the-object register on a permanent sign.

The plaque itself is the most three-dimensional in the whole wall: a row of small black metal springs is mounted directly into the white plaque face, with a blue inset panel holding the red Cree syllabics. nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak is carved in black above, with kîkwayak floated in blue to match the panel. Bed Springs sits at the bottom in matching blue. The combination reads as a 'physical pun' — the literal springs sit between the words for 'bed' and 'things that bounce'.

Bed Springs the mountain-bike trail runs through Patricia Ravine on Edmonton's southwest side, black-diamond rated, a short rooty ribbon that earns its name by the way the rooty fall-line section makes a rider's saddle 'sproing' off the pedals. The trail sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). The neighbouring trail in the same network is, fittingly, called Sproing! — same gag, same family of names.

notes: PHYSICAL SIGN OVERRIDES CATALOGUE: The carved plaque reads SRO nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak (with circumflexes on ê of nipêwin, â of kwâskwekotek, and î of kîkwayak). The current catalogue.json creeName is kekokel sôniyâwâhkêsis — that is in fact the Cree word for SILVERFOX and was accidentally placed on the Bed Springs entry. Coordinator should set bed-springs creeName to nipêwin ka kwâskwekotek kîkwayak and creeSyllabics to ᓂᐯᐃᐣ ᑲ ᑳᐢᑵᑯᑌᐠ ᑮᑿᔭᐠ.

The form ka kwâskwekotek is the relative / changed-conjunct of the II verb kwâskwêkotêw 'it bounces'. The plaque writes ka (short a) rather than kâ (long â) — both are attested in carved signage; kâ‑ is the standard descriptive-relative prefix. The internal vowels of kwâskwekotek on the plaque are short in places where standard published Cree would write kwâskwêkotêk. The fragment preserves the plaque spelling exactly; an alternate normalized spelling for educational use would be nipêwin kâ kwâskwêkotêk kîkway or ...kîkwayak.
Syllabic transcription ᓂᐯᐃᐣ for 'nipêwin' uses the bare ᐃ for the medial 'wi' rather than the more standard ᐏ; the carved plaque appears to use the simpler vowel glyph. Flagged for elder review.

culturalStory.heading: About the Silver Fox
body: The carved plaque reads sôniyâwâhkêsis — 'silver little-fox', the everyday Plains Cree way to name the rare silver-coated colour-phase of the red fox. sôniyâw is the same word for 'money', so the compound carries a soft double-reading: a 'money-fox', the kind of fox whose pelt was once worth a small fortune in the fur trade. The diminutive ‑âhkêsis is the bound, vowel-reduced version of the free NA noun mahkêsîs 'fox'.

The plaque art picks up the same poise — a stylized white-and-black silhouette of a fox in a flowing, kitsune-like pose, head turned and tail curling forward. The carving is mostly black on white with red syllabics. The English label is rendered as SILVEREFOX on this particular plaque (extra E between SILVER and FOX) — likely a layout/carving quirk; the catalogue and most signage use the more standard Silverfox.

Silver Fox the trail is a short descent in the Kinsmen / Emily Murphy network in Northwest Edmonton, ridden as part of the popular 'Shredders Kinsmen Loop' alongside nikocwâsaskanôs / Six Shooter and sâpwâpahcikan pâskisikan / Ray Gun. It sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory).

culturalStory.heading: About the Medicine Man
body: maskihkîwiyiniw is the everyday Plains Cree word for a healer — historically a traditional medicine person who carried plant knowledge, ceremony, and the responsibility of caring for the body, mind and spirit of the people. The word is built transparently: maskihkîw‑ 'of/with medicine' (the incorporated form of NI maskihkiy 'herb, medicine') + ‑iyiniw 'person, man'. The same headword now extends naturally to modern doctors and physicians as well — the noun did not need a new coining.

The plaque art tilts that double meaning forward: a clean, modern clinician — scrub cap, surgical mask, glasses — rendered in tidy black line-work with a blue scrub top and a blue surgical mask. The carved English label is the short, plain Medicine Man. The red syllabics carved above the figure spell ᒪᐢᑭᐦᑮᐏᔨᓂᐤ with the long ᑮ (kî) in the fifth-glyph position — the same long î that Trailforks itself uses on the trail's listing (maskihkîwiyiniw - Medicine Man).

Medicine Man the trail is a short, fast, black-diamond singletrack drop in the Hawrelak network on Edmonton's northwest side — 'just what the doctor ordered, a quick downhill through the trees' in the Trailforks description, with bank turns leading into Riverside Traverse. It sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory).

The current catalogue.json has maskihkiwiyiniw / ᒪᐢᑭᐦᑭᐏᔨᓂᐤ — both missing the long-î diacritic. The plaque's long-î form is independently confirmed by Trailforks' own listing for this trail (trailforks.com/trails/maskihkiwiyiniw-medicine-man/, which displays the name as ᒪᐢᑭᐦᑮᐃᐧᔨᓂᐤ - maskihkîwiyiniw - Medicine Man). culturalStory.heading: About the Little Sled
body: The plaque reads capanaskos — 'little sled', the diminutive of capanâsk 'toboggan, sled'. capanâsk is the Plains Cree noun for the wood-runner sled — the long flat sleigh historically pulled across the snow for hauling goods, game, and children — and the suffix ‑os shrinks it to the rider-sized 'bobsled' the trail is named for. The plaque's red toboggan-with-rider silhouette renders the diminutive literally: a small sled, a small bundled rider, ploughing down through a stylized stand of black evergreens against a snowy line.

Cree readers will notice that the carved spelling is capanaskos (short a in the third syllable), where a more standard published spelling would write capanâskos (long â). Both readings are attested in Plains Cree signage; the plaque preserves the shorter form. The red syllabics ᒐᐸᓇᐢᑯᐢ match the SRO carved above.

Bobsled the mountain-bike trail is a short, blue-rated downhill in the Hawrelak network on Edmonton's northwest side — a quick fall-line ribbon with a couple of line variations, drops, jumps, and berms, 'popular with downhillers' in the Trailforks description. It sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), in the same Hawrelak network as maskihkîwiyiniw / Medicine Man and kaskâwikanênêw / Back Breaker.

culturalStory.heading: The In‑Between Fire
body: In Catholic theology, purgatory is the in‑between place — neither heaven nor hell — where souls are held until they are purified by fire. The Plains Cree carved onto this plaque, kâsenamâkêw iskotêw, is a compact and quite precise calque of that idea: a fire (iskotêw) that refuses people (kâsenamâkêw 's/he refuses, rejects people' — itwêwina/Wolvengrey). It is the fire that holds you back at the threshold; the fire that says not yet.

Visually the plaque leans hard into that reading. Red and black flames frame the panel on both sides while a single white river meanders down the middle — souls funnelled between walls of fire, the cool white path threading between the heat. The Cree syllabics float above the flames in clean white block letters, the English 'Purgatory' anchors the bottom in red script. The four points/sparks above the syllabics read as embers, or possibly as stars — small fixed lights set against the moving fire below.

The trail itself is part of an Edmonton mountain‑bike sequence — sitting on the wall right beside paspîhiwêwin / 'Deliverance', which is the formally‑mapped Patricia Ravine Upper. Where Deliverance is the rescue out, Purgatory is the holding‑fire before it: same flame‑and‑river palette, opposite sides of the same theological hinge. The whole sequence is hung on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), and is part of an ongoing effort to put Plains Cree names back on the everyday landscape of Edmonton trails.

notes: PLAQUE SRO vs SYLLABICS INTERNAL MISMATCH: The plaque's carved Roman text reads 'kâsenamâkew iskotew' (no ê‑circumflex), while the carved syllabics ᑳᓭᓇᒫᑫᐤ ᐃᐢᑯᑌᐤ encode 'kâsênamâkêw iskotêw' (the syllabics ᓭ, ᑫ, ᑌ are by definition long‑ê). The page uses the linguistically‑correct SRO 'kâsenamâkêw iskotêw' (with circumflexes on ê) which matches the syllabics and the itwêwina headword kâsenamâkêw 's/he refuses, rejects people'. Catalogue currently reads 'kâsenamâkew iskotew' (no ê marks) — propose updating to 'kâsenamâkêw iskotêw' to keep SRO and syllabics in agreement, with the caveat that the physical plaque should be re‑carved at some future point to match.

Trailforks: no standalone match found for 'Purgatory'. The directory contains Patricia Ravine Upper = 'Deliverance' (id 13244) and Patricia Ravine Lower = 'Bed Springs', but no 'Purgatory'. The block intentionally renders the 'trail information coming soon' stub. If the trail builder confirms which sub‑section of Patricia Ravine they meant, we can link to that one.

kâsenamâkêw morpheme split: presented as kâseni‑ + ‑am‑ + ‑âkê‑ + ‑êw for teaching clarity. An alternative bracketing keeps ‑am‑âkê‑ as a single benefactive/indefinite‑object compound (the standard Plains Cree applicative). Either reading is defensible; the 4‑morpheme split is used here so each piece can be hover‑highlighted against the syllabics.

kâsenam vs. kâsîham: the page deliberately surfaces the near‑homophone 'kâsî‑ wipe / cleanse' because the design of the plaque (flames + a clean white river through the middle) reads strongly as a cleansing‑fire image even though the strict verb on the plaque is 'refuse'. culturalStory.heading: Through Patricia Ravine
body: In MTB vernacular a trail earns the name Deliverance by where it puts you and by what it asks of you to get out. On the wall, Deliverance sits paired with Purgatory — the same flame‑palette pivots into a wider banjo‑and‑bridge medallion, a winding pool of blue water threading underneath the bridge's pilings. The banjo is the John Boorman Deliverance reference (the 1972 film, the duelling‑banjos river); the bridge under it is the engineering of getting out alive. Black field, silver bridge, blue water, red Cree syllabics floating across the bridge deck — the design reads as a single rescue tableau.

The Cree carved onto the plaque, paspîhiwêwin, is the abstract noun of paspîhiwêw 's/he saves people' (itwêwina/Wolvengrey). The Plains Cree dictionary glosses it simply: rescue, saving people, deliverance, vindication. The same root paspî‑ 'slip through, escape, get out alive' is what makes paspiw 's/he survives' and paspâpiw 's/he peeks out through a hole' — the morpheme that runs through the whole family is the idea of getting through a narrow opening. That is also the literal shape of the trail: Patricia Ravine Upper, the black‑diamond singletrack threading through the steep, narrow ravine on Edmonton's west side.

Geographically the trail is the official 'Deliverance' on Trailforks (id 13244, Patricia Ravine Upper, 902 m, black diamond) — paired on the ground with 'Bed Springs' (Patricia Ravine Lower) and on the wall with 'Purgatory'. The whole sequence sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory) on the south rim of the North Saskatchewan, and is part of an Edmonton‑area effort to put Plains Cree names back onto the trails this network's riders have known by their English nicknames for a long time.

The plaque carved‑SRO drops the ê circumflex on 'we' (same pattern as the Purgatory plaque); the syllabics ᐍ (we, long‑ê by definition) implies the circumflex. itwêwina/Wolvengrey headword is 'paspîhiwêwin' with both diacritics.

body: Most of the plaques on this wall pair an English MTB trail name with a carved Plains Cree calque — sometimes a careful translation, sometimes a riff. The design source in the ewok/ folder is a hooded forest‑creature silhouette inspired by the Endor‑dwelling Ewoks of Return of the Jedi, and the trail itself appears to be a short, tight, low‑clearance forest section — the kind of trail where the rider hunches small to fit through, the way an Ewok moves through the trees of Endor.

We are not inventing a Cree name here — that would put words in the carvers' hands they did not choose to carve. If a Cree name is added later (the natural cultural analogue would be something built from memekwêsiw 'little forest being'), the page can be re‑drafted and the plaque eventually re‑carved. morphemes.gloss: Actor / agent nominalization prefix. Turns a VAI verb into the noun for the person who does that verb. Same prefix as in okimâw 'leader / one who leads' and opîkahtahkêw 'fiddler / one who fiddles'.
VAI stem: 'farm, plant, garden, seed, harvest'. Underlies the verb kistikêw 's/he farms / s/he plants'. itwêwina lists the agent noun okistikêw 'farmer' as a regular derivation.
VAI 3sg suffix carried into the actor noun: 's/he ___s' → 'the one who ___s'. The whole agent noun okistikêw = 'farmer / one who farms'.

Dependent kinship stem: 'daughter'. Cannot stand alone; always carries a possessor prefix. Compare nitânis 'my daughter', kitânis 'your daughter'.

Obviative suffix on the possessed animate noun. Required because the daughter (3rd person) is being talked about from the point of view of the farmer (also 3rd person). 'Two 3rd‑persons in the same clause' → one becomes obviative.

culturalStory.heading: The Field, the Daughter, the Trail
body: Farmer's Daughter is one of those MTB trail names that lives in the tradition of just calling it like you see it: a long, open, gently‑rolling line that feels like riding across the back forty of an old prairie farm, the kind a farmer's daughter would have grown up biking out to the field on. The plaque art leans straight into the trope — a sepia‑into‑purple portrait of a young woman on a battered single‑speed, white shirt and dark overalls, wheat in the background, the painted‑over‑a‑photograph aesthetic of an old farm‑family album. It is the most figurative plaque on the wall; almost every other one is a silhouette or an abstract motif.

The carved Cree above the portrait is precise: okistikêw otânisa, 'the farmer's daughter (obv.)'. okistikêw is the agent noun built from kistikêw 's/he farms, s/he plants' — strictly 'one who plants', so the kind of farm being named here is the planting / market‑garden / harvest kind, not the ranching kind (which would more naturally use otêhtêwâpêkinikêwa or similar). otânisa is the obviative form of otânis 'his/her daughter' — required because both the farmer and the daughter are 3rd‑person, and Plains Cree grammar marks one of them out as 'the other one' so listeners can keep track of who's who. The English possessive 's' has no machinery in Cree; the relationship rides entirely on the kinship stem ‑tânis 'daughter' carrying the same o‑ possessor as the farmer carries his actor o‑. Two o‑'s, two roles, one phrase.

Like every other plaque on this wall, the trail sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory). The Plains Cree had their own long history of kistikêwin (farming / cultivation) on this land — corn, squash, beans where the river bends, gathering and seasonal moves elsewhere — long before the homesteader idiom that 'Farmer's Daughter' borrows from. Naming the trail in nêhiyawêwin sets the English MTB nickname in conversation with that older history of working the land here.

culturalStory.heading: About kâkwa — the Porcupine
body: kâkwa (ᑳᑿ) is the Cree word for porcupine — a slow-moving, deeply self-possessed forest dweller of the boreal woods that stretch across nêhiyaw (Cree) territory. Unhurried and largely solitary, the porcupine is famously well-defended: rather than fight or flee, it lowers its head, raises its quills, and lets any aggressor make the mistake of pressing in. Cree teachings often hold up kâkwa as a quiet model of patience and gentle strength — protection through stillness rather than aggression, and the wisdom of knowing when not to move.

Long before glass beads arrived through the fur trade, porcupine quillwork was one of the most refined craft traditions of the Plains and Woodlands peoples, including the Cree. Quills were plucked, soaked, dyed with pigments drawn from roots, berries, lichens and ochres, then softened in the mouth, flattened with the teeth, and woven, wrapped, or sewn onto tanned hide, birchbark, moccasins, pipe stems, and lidded boxes. The geometric and floral patterns that later flourished in beadwork were first carried by quills — making kâkwa not only a forest neighbour but a literal source of artistic material, generously offered by an animal that asked only to be approached with care.

The red, black, and white of this trail sign carry an echo of those older quill-dye palettes — earth reds, charcoal blacks, and undyed natural whites that recur across many Indigenous quillwork traditions. (We note this resonance gently, as a visual rhyme rather than a claim about any specific tribal recipe.) Riding past kâkwa here in the river valley, it is worth pausing to remember an animal that taught generations of artists how to make beauty out of patience, and how to defend a small life with quiet, deliberate care.

culturalStory.heading: The Little One Who Looks (Like a Person)
body: Monkey is the English headline carved across the bottom of the plaque, but the larger Cree word painted across the body of the animal — ocayisinâkês — is where the linguistic interest lives. Plains Cree did not have monkeys in its pre‑contact ecological inventory, and so when monkeys arrived in the lexicon they arrived described rather than named: ocayisinâkês sits squarely on the productive ‑isinâkos‑ family of verbs and nouns of looking like / appearing as. The same final makes nipiy‑isinâkosiw 's/he looks watery' and maskoso‑isinâkosiw 's/he looks like a bear'. The ‑ês tail is the small‑animate diminutive — these are the little ones who look (a little) like a person. It is a word built by an Algonquian language doing exactly what Algonquian languages do when they meet a new animal: describe it from the inside out, by what it does or resembles, and let the noun fall out of the description.

Visually the plaque is one of the most direct on the wall: a clean black silhouette of a long‑tailed primate walking the length of the panel, red Cree syllabics ᐅᒐᔨᓯᓈᑫᐢ painted across its body, the English block‑letter MONKEY sitting underneath. Red‑on‑black‑on‑white is the working palette of this wall: black silhouettes for the animals, red for Cree, black for English. The monkey's curled tail is what makes it instantly read as 'monkey' rather than as any of the other species on the wall.

On the ground, 'Monkey' is one of the long‑standing nicknames for the Trailforks trail listed as Lovers Lane in Central Edmonton North (trail id 15796), with formal aliases Lovers Lane, Groat Road Roller Coaster, and Monkey Trail all on the same line. The trail winds through tight overhanging brush — the kind of tunnel‑of‑green section that earns names like monkey trail from riders who feel like they're swinging through the canopy. The trail sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory), and the carved ocayisinâkês is the local naming committee's choice for the Plains Cree word for the same idea.

morphemes.gloss: imitative initial: the open ‘oh‑’ that starts the howl. In Plains Cree, onomatopoeic animal-cry verbs often begin with an open vowel that mimics the very first sound the animal makes.

culturalStory.heading: About oyôyow — the Howl
body: Of all the trail signs in this set, oyôyow is the most audible. The word does not merely mean ‘howl’ — it is a howl, fixed into Cree morphology. The open ‘o‑’ opens the throat, the long ‘‑yô‑’ lifts and sustains the cry the way a wolf actually carries its voice across a river valley at dusk, and the falling ‘‑yo‑’ drops it back down before the final AI ending ‑w turns the whole imitation into a verb: ‘s/he howls.’ Plains Cree has a deep tradition of these imitative animal-cry verbs, and oyôyow is one of the cleanest examples.

On the wall the plaque hangs in two near-identical copies — the doubling is itself a kind of echo, the way a wolf-howl in the hills bounces back at you as a second voice. Each plaque shows the silhouette of a howling wolf in solid black, head tilted up, with the red syllabics ᐅᔫᔪᐤ set across the muzzle and chest so the language sits inside the animal it names. Underneath, the English ‘HOWL’ is laid out in a heavy block face: short, blunt, and onomatopoeic in its own sparse English way.

The trail itself sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory) in the Edmonton river-valley network — singletrack ridden by people who have known the line for decades by its English nickname and are now beginning to know it by the Cree word that names what the trail itself sounds like when you let off the brakes.

culturalStory.heading: About nôsemanicôs — the Female Little Bug
body: Across the prairies the ladybug carries an old reading as a small, marked, distinctly-female creature: brilliant red wing case, black head, polka-dot pattern that reads at any distance, and a habit of clustering on grass-stems where children can pick them up. The Cree name nôsemanicôs takes that reading literally — ‘female (nôse‑) little bug (manicôs).’ The same nôse‑ prefix that builds nôsemostos ‘cow’ (female buffalo) and nôsemâcêsis ‘doe’ shows up here on a tiny scale, marking the ladybug as the female-of-the-bug-family the way the cow is the female-of-the-bovine-family.

The plaque leans into that reading visually: a single red ladybug fills almost the whole white plaque, head turned, six legs splayed for balance, with the syllabics ᓅᓭᒪᓂᒎᐢ picked out in white across the polished red wing case so the language sits inside the body of the animal it names. White on red in 3D-printed PLA is the closest thing to red enamel paint with a dot of white pigment — exactly the colour scheme of the bug itself.

The trail of this name sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory) in the Edmonton river-valley network. Putting the diminutive feminine bug-word back onto an MTB sign places a Plains Cree linguistic micro-pattern (the productive nôse‑ prefix) onto a piece of the everyday landscape — small, polka-dotted, and easy to remember once you see how it is built.

culturalStory.heading: About victoria okimôtânimiyiwa — Victoria's Secret
body: The Edmonton trail named ‘Victoria's Secret’ is named for the small, lacy-looking line of the same nickname in the local MTB network — a piece of techy bench-cut singletrack that drops east-west along the river just south of the 102 Ave bridge, with off-camber roots, a couple of switchbacks, and a hidden, somewhat-private feel to it that earns the joke. The English name predates the plaque by years among the local riders who built and maintain the line; the Cree name victoria okimôtânimiyiwa reads that joke back through Plains Cree morphology.

Built up, the phrase is ‘Victoria, she keeps it secret from her (obviative)’: the borrowed name victoria followed by a fully-Cree VTA verb in obviative — the 3rd-person prefix o‑, the steal/stealth root kimôt‑, the ‑âni‑/‑m‑/‑iyi‑/‑wa relational tail that places the ‘her’ (the secret-keeper's secret) one degree further away than the agent. Plains Cree obviation lets the language pin down whose secret it is and whose it is from in a way English needs an extra ‘from’ for. The result is a phrase that reads as a small piece of grammar in motion: a proper noun handed to a verb that does the work of marking the secret as Victoria's own.

The plaque carries that reading visually as well. A black silhouette in the shape of a bra fills the pale-blue plaque, but the cups are not blank — they are filled with a forested pine-and-hill landscape with a small switchback path through it. The trail itself, in other words, is hidden inside the joke. Underneath, the carved Cree text victoria okimôtânimiyiwa and the English ‘Victoria's Secret’ run side-by-side. The trail sits on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory) in the Central Edmonton (North) river-valley network, near the Lovers Lane heart-plaque and the Wonder Woman silhouette — a small cluster of MTB-vernacular signs now also wearing a Plains Cree reading.

The verb has the unmistakable kimôt- (steal/stealth) root, the o- 3rd-person prefix, and the -iyi-/-wa obviative tail; the middle ‑âni‑/‑m‑ portion is treated here as stem-extender + VTA stem-marker for teaching clarity, but a stricter dictionary lookup may reanalyse it as a single ‑ânim‑ relational stem ('regard X as one's secret possession'). Either reading preserves the gloss 'she keeps it secret from her (obviative).'

Two near-identical 'Victoria's Secret' plaques are mounted on the wall (one on the upper-right cluster, one on the central-row cluster). The trail is part of the same river-valley cluster as Lovers Lane (#15796), Wonder Woman, and Purple Haze (#15797) — all of which appear on the wall as adjacent plaques. Sibling trails 'Victoria's Lower Secret' and 'Victoria's other secret' (#19734) also exist in the network but are clearly secondary spurs; the canonical 'Victoria's Secret' (#10632) is the line the plaque commemorates.

culturalStory.heading: About slinky — the Sculpture That Is the Sign
body: Of the twenty-plus pieces on this wall, slinky is the only one where the trail-sign installation IS the artefact rather than a plaque about the artefact. A roughly four-foot-tall continuous red wire spring — recognisably a giant scaled-up version of Richard James's 1945 coil-toy — drops from row 1 down through row 3, threading between the other plaques, with a small white companion plaque tucked in at the top-left carrying the English word ‘slinky’ in raised black letters and a red syllabic transliteration of the loanword underneath. There is no carved Plains Cree calque, because the spring-toy is itself a borrowed English name with no Cree equivalent: the sculpture is the word.

The trail it commemorates sits in the Central Edmonton (South) / Keillor river-valley network on ᓀᐦᐃᔭᐤ ᐊᐢᑭᕀ Nêhiyaw‑Askiy (Plains Cree territory) and is actually a small family of three — Slinky - North (Trailforks #51286, ~2,221 ft of typical river's-edge singletrack), Slinky - Mid (#150113, the short ‘best section of the three Slinkys’), and a Slinky - South sister line. Strung end-to-end the three sections do, in fact, read on the map as a coil that recoils back on itself — flat, off-camber, jumbly — which is why the riders who built and named the line gave it the toy's name.

Plains Cree handles spring-like motion descriptively rather than with a single noun. The verb kwêskwêkotêw ‘it bounces, it coils and springs back’ — the same root the wall uses on the Bed Springs plaque (nipêwin ka kwêskwêkotêk kikwayak ‘the thing that bounces on a bed’) — paired with piwâpisk ‘metal’ gives a transparent Cree paraphrase ‘bouncy metal thing,’ but the builders of this wall chose instead to leave the slinky as itself: the loanword stays, the sculpture does the talking.
